title: API and boundaries
summary: Name client operations and the service boundary that owns each one.

parts.rule: List the external operations as HTTP-style verbs and paths or as RPCs. For each operation, name the service that owns the truth for that write. Keep boundaries aligned with data ownership so two services never both believe they are the source of truth for the same field. Prefer coarse resources over chatty micro-endpoints in the first sketch.
parts.why: Fuzzy ownership creates dual writes and circular call graphs. Sketches that jump to internals without an API leave the client contract undefined. A crisp boundary list also reveals which calls must stay synchronous on the user path and which may move to a queue.
parts.example: Ride-hailing MVP APIs: POST /trips for a rider request, POST /trips/{id}/accept for a driver, POST /trips/{id}/complete, and GET /trips/{id}. Ownership: Trip Service owns trip state; Location Service owns driver positions; Billing Service owns charges. Accept is a write inside Trip Service; it may read Location but must not let Location mutate trip status. Reject a design where Trip and Dispatch both update a trip status column independently. For a URL shortener, GET /{code} is owned by Redirect reading the links row; POST /v1/links is owned by Link Service. Sharing one database early is fine; the API still names a single writer path per operation so later splits stay honest.
parts.use: Draft the API right after requirements. Use it to assign ownership before drawing arrows between boxes. Use boundaries to decide which calls may be async via a queue versus synchronous on the user path.

body:
Rule. List the external operations as HTTP-style verbs and paths or as RPCs. For each operation, name the service that owns the truth for that write. Keep boundaries aligned with data ownership so two services never both believe they are the source of truth for the same field. Prefer coarse resources over chatty micro-endpoints in the first sketch.

Why it matters. Fuzzy ownership creates dual writes and circular call graphs. Sketches that jump to internals without an API leave the client contract undefined. A crisp boundary list also reveals which calls must stay synchronous on the user path and which may move to a queue.

Worked example. Ride-hailing MVP APIs: POST /trips for a rider request, POST /trips/{id}/accept for a driver, POST /trips/{id}/complete, and GET /trips/{id}. Ownership: Trip Service owns trip state; Location Service owns driver positions; Billing Service owns charges. Accept is a write inside Trip Service; it may read Location but must not let Location mutate trip status. Reject a design where Trip and Dispatch both update a trip status column independently. For a URL shortener, GET /{code} is owned by Redirect reading the links row; POST /v1/links is owned by Link Service. Sharing one database early is fine; the API still names a single writer path per operation so later splits stay honest.

[[diagram:boundary]]

When to use. Draft the API right after requirements. Use it to assign ownership before drawing arrows between boxes. Use boundaries to decide which calls may be async via a queue versus synchronous on the user path.

When to refuse. Refuse ten microservices for five endpoints on day one. Refuse two writers for one authoritative field. Refuse undocumented side effects such as accept also billing without naming that call. Refuse designing internal tables before any client operation exists.
